name: LGD-3303
lead: LGD-3303 is an investigational, orally available nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals, with a tricyclic pyrrolo[3,2-f]quinolin-7-one structure [1][2]. SARMs as a class are designed to activate the androgen receptor in muscle and bone more than in reproductive tissue such as the prostate, so the appearance-related interest is the chain from androgen-receptor activation to more muscle and bone mass and a more muscular physique [6]. In rats, LGD-3303 increased muscle weight and bone mineral density [2][3].

Published work on LGD-3303 consists of animal and in vitro studies of its pharmacokinetics, muscle and bone effects and effects on sexual behaviour in female rats [2][3][4]. No registered human trial was found, and it is not approved for any use [1]. SARMs are prohibited in sport, and detection studies of LGD-3303 metabolites in horses have been published [1][5][7]. In bodybuilding forums the compound is mentioned mainly in lists of SARMs rather than as a widely used product [8][9].

paras: SARMs activate the androgen receptor selectively, aiming to build muscle and bone with fewer effects on tissues such as the prostate. They were conceived as an alternative to anabolic androgenic steroids, whose side effects limit medical use. Most are nonsteroidal, and as of Wikipedia's 2023 update neither the FDA nor the European Medicines Agency had approved any SARM [6]. The first nonsteroidal SARMs were developed in 1998 by two groups, one at the University of Tennessee and one at Ligand Pharmaceuticals, which used a quinolone core. The term SARM was introduced in 1999 by analogy with SERMs [6].

Hypotheses for tissue selectivity include that SARMs are not converted by 5-alpha-reductase to a more potent form as testosterone is, and that differences in coactivator and corepressor recruitment make them full agonists in muscle and bone but partial agonists in the prostate. Autoradiography with other SARMs did not support preferential accumulation in muscle [6].

LGD-3303 is named 9-chloro-2-ethyl-1-methyl-3-(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl)-3H-pyrrolo[3,2-f]quinolin-7(6H)-one and has the formula C16H14ClF3N2O [1][2]. It belongs to a series of nonsteroidal androgen receptor ligands built by Ligand Pharmaceuticals on quinolinone templates; related compounds include LGD-2226 and LGD-2941, and LGD-4033 is a separate chemotype [1]. A 2010 paper describes LGD-3303 as nonsteroidal, nonaromatizable, highly selective for the androgen receptor and able to cross the blood-brain barrier [4].

In castrated male rats, LGD-3303 showed potent activity on the levator ani muscle with partial agonist activity on the prostate and preputial gland. Prostate weight stayed at or below intact-animal levels as plasma concentrations rose, whether the compound was given orally or by continuous infusion [1][2]. Authors of the 2009 study interpreted tissue selectivity as arising from receptor-level interactions rather than differences in tissue distribution [1][2]. In vitro, it was described as a potent nonsteroidal androgen with little or no cross-reactivity with related nuclear receptors [3].

After oral administration of 0.05 mg per kg to horses, researchers identified eight metabolites in plasma and urine and proposed a monohydroxylated metabolite as a doping-control target because of its intensity and longer detection time [5]. An equine liver-microsome study of seven SARMs found four phase I metabolites for LGD-3303 [7]. The compound is described as prohibited in equine and human sport [5].

No studies found in humans. Published work is limited to animals and cell systems. In ovariectomized female rats, LGD-3303 increased muscle weight and bone mineral density at cortical and cancellous sites and combined additively with the bisphosphonate alendronate [3]. In gonadectomized female rats given 3 to 30 mg per kg by oral gavage, it enhanced male-directed sexual preference only in sexually experienced animals [4]. A ClinicalTrials.gov search returned no records for it [1].

No human safety data were identified for LGD-3303. For the SARM class, randomised trials have reported mild and infrequent adverse events, while case reports link recreational use to drug-induced liver injury, and SARMs can raise liver enzymes, lower HDL cholesterol and reduce gonadotropins and testosterone in a dose- and compound-dependent way [6]. The FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot be legally marketed as supplements or drugs, and has reported liver injury and cardiovascular events for the class [1]. WADA banned SARMs in 2008 [6].

Outside research, SARMs are a gray-market category sold as research chemicals, popular with bodybuilders and athletes, and a study cited on Wikipedia found most products advertised online as SARMs were mislabelled [6]. On T Nation, LGD-3303 appears in lists of preclinical SARMs in a thread on ostarine, and in a 2009 thread a member asks whether anyone had information about it [8][9].

Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic and bone-combination studies in rats published [2][3].

Equine in vitro metabolism of seven SARMs including LGD-3303 published [7].
Equine in vivo metabolite profiling for doping control published [5].

card.summary: A Ligand Pharmaceuticals nonsteroidal SARM tested only in rats and horses; no human data.
card.note: Preclinical only; banned in sport; unapproved.

quick.overview:
LGD-3303 is an experimental SARM made by Ligand Pharmaceuticals. Animal studies looked at its effects on muscle, bone and female sexual behaviour.

No human trial has been registered, so its effects in people are unknown.
quick.mechanism: It activates the androgen receptor; in rats it stimulated muscle strongly while only partially stimulating prostate tissue.
quick.risks: There are no human safety data. SARMs as a class are unapproved, banned in sport, and linked in reports to liver injury.

chain: Oral SARM binds the androgen receptor
Greater activity in muscle and bone than in prostate in rat models
Increased lean muscle and bone density (rats); no human data
angle.text: As a SARM, LGD-3303 is designed to give androgen-like muscle effects with less effect on the prostate. In castrated male rats it was potent on the levator ani muscle, and in ovariectomized female rats it increased muscle weight and bone density; no human results exist.
